In which we first must ask "What is reality?"

There need be some operating parameters to our definitions. "Reality" is being inquired against, therefore we cannot use itself as the definition for it would be circular. We cannot use our interactions with it as its definition either, except insofar as those interactions can be said to posses qualities which are extant in all other interactions. I.e. a consistent nature.

Why is it we seek a consistent nature? Think briefly upon the problem of any given object, where though we each see an object we do not in fact see its identical qualities. Though an object must exist for us to see qualities from, those qualities are dependent upon the observer. Therefore, only such qualities which can be said to be consistent across all observations may be considered part of a "true nature" belonging to the object itself. Most commonly that "X object is in Y position", even though we perceive positions differently.

Therefore to do this requires some level of empirical thought. We determine what is true by repetition, examining the conditions and results of that repetition, and extrapolating from this a part of this nature of our reality. That is to say, the reality in which we mutually observe from different points.

So we achieve a process in this by which we can agree on a few points. "A" reality does exist, for there are certain qualities which are so tested as to probably exist everywhere. While we cannot be absolutely certain, we can be reasonably so by experiment. We can further state we exist in the same reality, for though we receive different "inputs" those inputs come from the same source. If those were not from the same source, a given consistent law would alter our shared experience differently. Or possibly that we are not, truly, undergoing the same shared experience.

We can then suppose that what reality "is", in an objective sense, is composed of definitive rules known and unknown which affect our perceptions of it consistently. Although two given people may perceive the same phenomenon with different meaning, those two still observe A given phenomenon.

Let us further suppose another proof of concept. For we also know the inverse, that of an inconsistent reality, by means of our dreams. In our subjective lives we differentiate between the two entirely by knowing what inconsistent reality would look like. Were both entirely consistent, there would be no means to know their difference, and nobody could truly be said to be "awake". Neither capable of determining which is real.

Although it is then defined that reality is then a "consistent" point of reference across all points, in that we can agree "A phenomenon exists all points can observe", there is a further question. Why do we choose to believe in a consistent reality instead of an inconsistent one? A consistent reality proves incredibly boring once consistency is achieved, while an inconsistent reality is one of chaos.

Therefore we may also conclude that "We know this to be real because we know what is not real". For what is not real, though its origin may have qualities observable (An fMRI of a dreaming mind), the products of its observations are chaotic and subjective. It further cannot influence bodies outside of its subjective set.

So what is real can be observed by all within the set of observables called "reality", as well as influence it in kind with its qualities. What is not real can only interact from within its own subset within reality, and only be observed in kind by its causation from reality.
